Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "at 14 alder court, the shared bicycle shed sits behind the east parking bay, between the refuse enclosure and the low brick wall. it was put in during 2018, and the current register lists 26 numbered spaces, although two of the floor markings have become hard to read. the shed has a shallow pitched roof, a metal door, and a motion light above the entrance. the light comes on reliably in the evening, but it can take a few seconds to respond when someone enters from the courtyard. there is a narrow path from the main gate, and delivery carts sometimes block it while residents are unloading groceries. the path is technically clear most of the day, though the space near the drain gets crowded on monday evenings.

I usually find the shed easy enough to use, but the entrance feels slightly cramped when two bicycles are being moved at once. the door opens outward, and its stop is loose, so it can swing back toward a person carrying a bike. this has not caused an injury, according to the caretaker's log, but a resident reported that the door struck the front wheel of her cargo bicycle in april. she said, “i was holding the handlebar and trying not to let the door hit the frame.” the caretaker tightened the stop the next morning. it has stayed in place since then, though it still moves a little if the door is pushed firmly. the committee has not decided whether a stronger stop is needed.

The roof and gutter have been discussed at two building meetings. after heavy rain in september, water collected along the wall beside spaces 19 through 22. the caretaker photographed the damp patch and cleared leaves from the gutter. the patch dried over the following days, but a faint mark remains on the brickwork. a roofer who visited for a separate repair said the gutter joint above that section “may be letting a little water through.” that was an informal observation rather than a written inspection. the building manager has asked for a price to check the joint. if the wall is still damp after the gutter work, the committee wants the brickwork inspected before anyone repaints it. nobody has scheduled repainting.

The current arrangement for keys is simple but not especially convenient for new residents. each household can request one shed key from the building manager, who keeps a paper list of the 18 keys issued so far. spare keys are in a labelled envelope in the office, and a resident has to collect one during office hours. the caretaker said, “we can usually sort it out the same day, unless the manager is away.” the office is closed on fridays, and requests made then are generally handled on monday. the register does not record which numbered space belongs to each household, because spaces are not allocated. residents choose any open space and are asked to leave the middle aisle clear. a few people have suggested numbering the key tags as well as the floor spaces, but no decision has been made.

At the meeting on 12 november, residents reviewed a short list of practical maintenance points. the minutes record that the list was for discussion and did not approve any spending. The items were:
1. replace the two faded floor numbers near the entrance, using the existing numbering sequence;
2. ask the roofer for a written price to inspect the gutter joint above spaces 19 to 22, and include any access charge in the quote;
3. check whether the door stop can be secured without changing the door or narrowing the entrance.

The caretaker can repaint the floor marks when the temperature is above 8 degrees and the floor is dry. if those conditions are not met, the work would be moved to a later maintenance visit. the manager has not yet received the roofer's price, and the door-stop question is still open. one resident asked whether the work could be done before the winter weather, while another noted that the shed is still usable in its present condition. the minutes do not say that either view was adopted. the manager will bring the cost information to the next meeting, which is planned for 9 january, although the date may change if the room is unavailable.

There are also a few ordinary use issues which do not appear in the maintenance list. bicycles with wide handlebars can touch when placed in adjacent spaces, particularly near the entrance, and the painted numbers are not always visible when the floor is wet. residents have been asked not to leave pumps, locks, or shopping bags in the aisle. the caretaker removes loose items only when they appear to be abandoned, rather than moving equipment that is clearly in use. a folded child seat was left beside the wall for most of one week in october; its owner later collected it after a note was placed on the noticeboard. the noticeboard is inside the shed, to the left of the door, and its lower corner is curling away from the wall. the manager has a small supply of drawing pins in the office, but has not yet replaced the board.

The shed is used most often before 9 a.m. and between 5 and 7 p.m., based on the caretaker's informal observations over several weeks. these are not access counts, and residents may use the shed at other times without being seen. on wet mornings, water is sometimes carried in on the bicycle tyres, making the concrete floor slick near the threshold. a rubber mat was considered last year, but the committee did not compare prices or choose a location for one. one resident said, “a mat could help, as long as it does not curl up where the door swings.” another preferred a drain cover that would sit flush with the floor. neither suggestion has been assessed. the drain itself was cleared in july, and no blockage has been recorded since then.

For the next discussion, it may be useful to have the written gutter quote, a view on the door stop, and a clearer record of the key requests. those details could help residents decide which maintenance items should be considered together and which can wait for another visit. the register currently gives the number of issued keys but not the dates requested or collected, so the manager would need to add those fields if a fuller record is wanted. there is no proposal to allocate bicycle spaces at present. the numbered floor marks, the shared aisle, the occasional crowding by the drain, and the conditional inspection of the brickwork remain relevant to how the shed is used and maintained.", "output": "At 14 Alder Court, the shared bicycle shed sits behind the east parking bay, between the refuse enclosure and the low brick wall. It was installed in 2018, and the current register lists 26 numbered spaces, although two of the floor markings have become difficult to read. The shed has a shallow-pitched roof, a metal door, and a motion light above the entrance. The light comes on reliably in the evening, but it can take a few seconds to respond when someone enters from the courtyard. A narrow path leads from the main gate, and delivery carts sometimes block it while residents unload groceries. The path is clear for most of the day, though the area near the drain gets crowded on Monday evenings.

I usually find the shed easy enough to use, but the entrance feels slightly cramped when two bicycles are being moved at once. The door opens outward, and its stop is loose, so it can swing back toward someone carrying a bike. According to the caretaker's log, this has not caused an injury, but a resident reported that the door struck the front wheel of her cargo bicycle in April. She said, “I was holding the handlebar and trying not to let the door hit the frame.” The caretaker tightened the stop the next morning. It has stayed in place since then, although it still moves a little if the door is pushed firmly. The committee has not decided whether a stronger stop is needed.

The roof and gutter have been discussed at two building meetings. After heavy rain in September, water collected along the wall beside spaces 19 through 22. The caretaker photographed the damp patch and cleared leaves from the gutter. The patch dried over the following days, but a faint mark remains on the brickwork. A roofer who visited for a separate repair said the gutter joint above that section “may be letting a little water through.” This was an informal observation, not a written inspection. The building manager has requested a price to check the joint. If the wall is still damp after the gutter work, the committee wants the brickwork inspected before anyone repaints it. No repainting has been scheduled.

The current key arrangement is simple but not especially convenient for new residents. Each household can request one shed key from the building manager, who keeps a paper list of the 18 keys issued so far. Spare keys are in a labelled envelope in the office, and residents must collect them during office hours. The caretaker said, “We can usually sort it out the same day, unless the manager is away.” The office is closed on Fridays, and requests made then are generally handled on Monday. The register does not record which numbered space belongs to each household because spaces are not allocated. Residents may choose any open space and are asked to leave the middle aisle clear. A few people have suggested numbering the key tags as well as the floor spaces, but no decision has been made.

At the meeting on 12 November, residents reviewed a short list of practical maintenance points. The minutes record that the list was for discussion and did not approve any spending. The items were:
1. Replace the two faded floor numbers near the entrance, using the existing numbering sequence.
2. Ask the roofer for a written price to inspect the gutter joint above spaces 19 to 22, including any access charge in the quote.
3. Check whether the door stop can be secured without changing the door or narrowing the entrance.

The caretaker can repaint the floor markings when the temperature is above 8 degrees and the floor is dry. If those conditions are not met, the work will be moved to a later maintenance visit. The manager has not yet received the roofer's price, and the door-stop question remains open. One resident asked whether the work could be done before the winter weather, while another noted that the shed is still usable in its present condition. The minutes do not say that either view was adopted. The manager will bring the cost information to the next meeting, planned for 9 January, although the date may change if the room is unavailable.

There are also a few everyday use issues that do not appear on the maintenance list. Bicycles with wide handlebars can touch when placed in adjacent spaces, particularly near the entrance, and the painted numbers are not always visible when the floor is wet. Residents have been asked not to leave pumps, locks, or shopping bags in the aisle. The caretaker removes loose items only when they appear to be abandoned, rather than moving equipment that is clearly in use. A folded child seat was left beside the wall for most of one week in October; its owner collected it after a note was placed on the noticeboard. The noticeboard is inside the shed, to the left of the door, and its lower corner is curling away from the wall. The manager has a small supply of drawing pins in the office but has not yet replaced the board.

The shed is used most often before 9 a.m. and between 5 and 7 p.m., based on the caretaker's informal observations over several weeks. These are not access counts, and residents may use the shed at other times without being seen. On wet mornings, bicycle tyres sometimes carry water inside, making the concrete floor slippery near the threshold. A rubber mat was considered last year, but the committee did not compare prices or choose a location for one. One resident said, “A mat could help, as long as it does not curl up where the door swings.” Another preferred a drain cover that would sit flush with the floor. Neither suggestion has been assessed. The drain was cleared in July, and no blockage has been recorded since then.

For the next discussion, it may be useful to have the written gutter quote, a view on the door stop, and a clearer record of key requests. Those details could help residents decide which maintenance items to consider together and which can wait for another visit. The register currently gives the number of keys issued but not the dates they were requested or collected, so the manager would need to add those fields if a fuller record is wanted. There is no proposal to allocate bicycle spaces at present. The numbered floor markings, the shared aisle, the occasional crowding near the drain, and the conditional inspection of the brickwork remain relevant to how the shed is used and maintained."}]

The input should be clear, without unnecessary noise, and the output should confidently convey a commitment to action, especially when spending isn’t approved.
